es.summary: Los bloqueadores beta inhiben los receptores β‑adrenérgicos, reduciendo la frecuencia y fuerza del latido y la liberación de renina.
key_points: Disminuyen la frecuencia cardíaca y la contractilidad miocárdica.
Son esenciales en hipertensión, insuficiencia cardíaca y angina.
Los no selectivos pueden provocar broncoespasmo en asmáticos.
No deben suspenderse abruptamente para evitar rebote de taquicardia.

mechanism: Bloquean receptores β1 en corazón y riñón → ↓ frecuencia, contractilidad y renina.
Bloqueo β2 (no selectivos) impide broncodilatación → riesgo de broncoespasmo.
Algunos poseen actividad α‑bloqueante, favoreciendo vasodilatación.
indications: Angina de pecho y prevención post‑infarto.
Arritmias supraventriculares y control de frecuencia en fibrilación auricular.
contraindications: Bloqueo AV de segundo o tercer grado sin marcapasos.
interactions: Potenciación de hipotensión con otros antihipertensivos.
Bradicardia aumentada con calcio‑antagonistas y digoxina.
Prolongación del intervalo PR con antiarrítmicos de clase IA/IB.
Mascaramiento de síntomas hipoglucémicos con insulina y sulfonilureas.
Los AINEs pueden reducir el efecto antihipertensivo.
nursing_care: Evaluar frecuencia cardíaca y presión arterial antes de administrar; retener si HR <60 lpm o PA sistólica <90 mmHg.
Monitorear ECG y signos de insuficiencia cardíaca durante la terapia.
Observar respiración; suspender si aparece sibilancia o dificultad respiratoria (no selectivos).
Controlar glucosa en pacientes diabéticos; informar signos de hipoglucemia.
Registrar posición al levantarse; observar mareos por hipotensión ortostática.
patient_teaching: Tomar la dosis a la misma hora cada día; no interrumpir sin orden médica.
Informar al profesional si presenta mareos, fatiga extrema o dificultad para respirar.
Evitar consumo de alcohol y actividades que requieran alerta inmediata hasta conocer su respuesta.
En caso de asma o enfermedad pulmonar, avisar al médico antes de iniciar terapia.
No usar en caso de embarazo sin indicación específica; consultar siempre.

en.summary: Beta blockers inhibit β‑adrenergic receptors, reducing heart rate, contractility, and renin release.
key_points: Reduce heart rate and myocardial contractility.
Essential for hypertension, heart failure, and angina.
Non‑selective agents can cause bronchospasm in asthmatics.
Abrupt discontinuation should be avoided to prevent tachycardia rebound.

mechanism: Block β1 receptors in heart and kidney → ↓ heart rate, contractility, and renin.
β2 blockade (non‑selective) prevents bronchodilation → risk of bronchospasm.
Some have α‑blocking activity, favoring vasodilation.
indications: Supraventricular arrhythmias and rate control in atrial fibrillation.
contraindications: Second or third‑degree AV block without pacemaker.
interactions: Potentiation of hypotension with other antihypertensives.
Increased bradycardia with calcium channel blockers and digoxin.
PR interval prolongation with class IA/IB antiarrhythmics.
Masking of hypoglycemic symptoms with insulin and sulfonylureas.
nursing_care: Assess heart rate and blood pressure before administration; hold if HR <60 bpm or systolic BP <90 mmHg.
Monitor ECG and signs of heart failure during therapy.
Observe breathing; discontinue if wheezing or respiratory distress appears (non‑selective).
Check glucose in diabetic patients; report hypoglycemia signs.
Record position upon standing; watch for dizziness from orthostatic hypotension.
patient_teaching: Take the dose at the same time each day; do not stop without medical order.
Inform provider if you experience dizziness, extreme fatigue, or breathing difficulty.
Avoid alcohol and activities requiring alertness until you know your response.
If you have asthma or lung disease, notify your doctor before starting therapy.
Do not use during pregnancy unless specifically indicated; always consult a professional.

summary.0.quote: Beta blockers decrease heart rate, decrease myocardial contractility, and decrease the rate of conduction through the atrioventricular (AV) node, thereby lowering blood pressure and heart rate.

key_points.0.quote: Beta blockers decrease heart rate, decrease myocardial contractility, and decrease the rate of conduction through the atrioventricular (AV) node, thereby lowering blood pressure and heart rate.

key_points.1.quote: Beta blockers treat clients with hypertension, heart failure, arrhythmias, myocardial infarctions, migraines, glaucoma, and certain types of tremors.

sections.mechanism.0.quote: Beta 1 receptors are found primarily in the heart and kidneys, and they increase the heart rate, myocardial activity, and release of renin.

sections.indications.0.quote: Indications To control hypertension In the treatment of angina, acute myocardial infarction, and heart failure

sections.indications.1.quote: Indications To control hypertension In the treatment of angina, acute myocardial infarction, and heart failure

sections.indications.2.quote: Indications To control hypertension In the treatment of angina, acute myocardial infarction, and heart failure

sections.contraindications.3.quote: Beta blockers are contraindicated in clients with moderate to severe asthma and/or chronic lung diseases due to the potential for causing an exacerbation.

sections.adverse_effects.0.quote: Adverse Effects Fatigue/weakness Dizziness Headache Hypotension Blur

sections.adverse_effects.2.quote: Adverse effects of beta blockers are dizziness, fatigue, weight gain, constipation, cold hands and feet, hypercholesterolemia, shortness of breath, depression, nausea, dry mouth, and dry eyes.

sections.adverse_effects.3.quote: Rare side effects include sexual and erectile dysfunction.

sections.adverse_effects.5.quote: People with diabetes should use beta blockers cautiously because they can mask the symptoms of hypoglycemia, causing confusion, fainting, or seizures.

sections.interactions.3.quote: People with diabetes should use beta blockers cautiously because they can mask the symptoms of hypoglycemia, causing confusion, fainting, or seizures.

sections.patient_teaching.1.quote: Report side effects such as bradycardia, hypotension, fatigue, dizziness, constipation, or sexual dysfunction to their health care provider.
